hook: Miss your **compiler**? Good news — Python can have compile-time safety too. Optional, gradual, and free.

scenes.title: Annotate the **shape**, keep the freedom
scenes.sub: Hints are for readers and checkers — Python ignores them at runtime
scenes.narration: Type hints are annotations — colons and arrows that describe what a function takes and returns. Python itself ignores them completely at runtime; the power comes from external checkers that read your code statically. That means you get C sharp-style safety without giving up Python's flexibility — and you can adopt it gradually, file by file, function by function.

lines: def add(a: int, b: int) {{-> int}}:

steps.at: an arrow before the return type

scenes.narration: The syntax: name colon type, and an arrow before the return type. Collections take parameters in square brackets — list of string, dict of string to int. And a modernization note: before Python 3.9 you imported capital-L List from typing; today lowercase builtins are the standard. If you see capital versions in older codebases, that's the reason.

scenes.title: **Optional[X]** = X or None

steps.at: you must say Optional of string
checker will then force every caller

scenes.narration: In C sharp, string can be null unless you enable nullable reference types. In Python-with-hints, the rule is explicit: a parameter typed string does not accept None — if None is legal, you must say Optional of string, which means string or None. The checker will then force every caller to handle the None case. This one annotation eliminates the most common runtime crash in the language.

actors.t: feels like getting the compiler back

steps.at: if a value might be None
do: x may be None  ✗ red squiggle

scenes.narration: Unions say 'either'. Modern syntax: string pipe int. The checker tracks every path: if a value might be None, calling a string method on it is a red squiggle, not a production incident. Combined with isinstance narrowing — if isinstance of x comma string — the checker understands your guard and clears the error. It genuinely feels like getting the compiler back.

scenes.title: Generics: **write once, type forever**
scenes.sub: TypedDict: give your dicts a shape

steps.at: gives a dictionary a fixed schema
shape of every LLM API payload

scenes.narration: Generics parameterize functions and classes over types — T in C sharp, TypeVar in Python. One function, first of list of T, type-checks for lists of anything while keeping the element type. And TypedDict is the gem you'll actually use daily: it gives a dictionary a fixed schema — which keys exist, what types they hold — which is precisely the shape of every LLM API payload you'll handle.

do: a dict with a known shape

steps.at: if the data is JSON throughout

scenes.narration: Two tools, one choice. Generics with a type parameter T: write first, get first of strings, first of ints, all type-checked. TypedDict declares schemas for data that stays a dict — API responses, tool arguments. And the boundary: if the data is JSON throughout, TypedDict; if it's a real object with behavior, dataclass or Pydantic. Knowing which side of that line you're on is a senior signal.

scenes.title: mypy & pyright: **your new compiler**
scenes.sub: Run them in CI, watch them in your editor

actors.t: editor: red squiggles as you type
CI: type errors can never merge

scenes.narration: The two mainstream checkers: mypy — the original, runs as a command line tool, great in CI. Pyright — Microsoft's engine, powers Pylance in VS Code, extremely fast with the best error messages. Either is fine; pyright if you live in VS Code. Wire one into your editor for red squiggles as you type, and into CI so type errors can never merge. Start lenient, tighten gradually.

lines: # CI: fail the build on any error

actors.t: one CI line makes it real

steps.at: One CI line makes it real

scenes.narration: Adoption path. Day one: run mypy loose, only on your code. Week two: require annotations on new functions — disallow untyped defs. Then tighten toward strict. The trap to avoid: annotating half a codebase and ignoring the checker output. Types are a contract; an unenforced contract is just decoration. One CI line makes it real — mypy, and fail the build.

recap: Hints: name: type -> return; collections parameterize as list[str]
Optional[str] = str | None — declare None or the checker complains at callers
TypedDict for dict-shaped data; mypy/pyright in editor + CI, tighten gradually

opts: The parameter is optional (can be omitted)
The value is str or None
quiz.why: Optional[X] = X | None. 'Can be omitted' is what a default value expresses — a different thing.

quiz.q: When is TypedDict the right choice over dataclass?
opts: When you need methods on the object
When the data must remain a plain dict (e.g. JSON payloads)
When you need validation of values
quiz.why: TypedDict types dicts in place — perfect for API/JSON-shaped data. Real objects with behavior → dataclass/Pydantic.

quiz.q: Do type hints change how Python runs?
opts: No — Python ignores them at runtime; checkers use them statically
quiz.why: Hints are inert at runtime. The safety comes from mypy/pyright analyzing the code before it runs.

code.title: Type hints that earn their keep
code.body:
from typing import TypedDict, Optional

# --- basics ---------------------------------------------------
def estimate_cost(model: str, tokens: int) -> float:
    prices: dict[str, float] = {"gpt-4o": 2.50, "sonnet": 3.00}
    return tokens / 1_000_000 * prices.get(model, 1.00)

# --- Optional: None must be declared ---------------------------
def find_model(name: str) -> Optional[str]:
    return name if name.startswith("gpt") else None

m = find_model("gpt-4o")
if m is not None:                 # narrowing — mypy verifies this guard
    print(m.upper())

# --- TypedDict: schemas for dict-shaped data -------------------
class ChatMessage(TypedDict):
    role: str
    content: str

class ApiResponse(TypedDict):
    model: str
    message: ChatMessage
    tokens: int

payload: ApiResponse = {
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "message": {"role": "assistant", "content": "hi"},
    "tokens": 12,
}

# --- check -----------------------------------------------------
# $ pip install mypy
# $ mypy --ignore-missing-imports src/
# CI: mypy src/ && pytest          # types gate + tests gate
annot: prices.get(model, 1.00) — a default beats Optional handling for lookup-style dicts
`if m is not None` narrowing: mypy knows m is str inside the block
TypedDicts nest — ApiResponse contains a ChatMessage, fully checked

notes:
# Type Hints

## Basics
- `def f(name: str, n: int = 1) -> str:` — params + return.
- Collections parameterize: `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]`, `tuple[str, int]`.
- Modern (3.9+): lowercase builtins; legacy code uses `typing.List` etc.

## Optional & Union
- `Optional[str]` ≡ `str | None` — None must be **declared**.
- `str | int` (3.10+) / `Union[str, int]`.
- Narrow with `if x is not None:` / `isinstance(...)` — checkers understand guards.

## Generics & TypedDict
```python
def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T:   # 3.12+ (TypeVar before 3.12)
    return items[0]

class ApiResponse(TypedDict):
    model: str
    tokens: int
```
- **TypedDict** = dict with a schema (JSON land) · **dataclass/Pydantic** = real objects.

## mypy / pyright
- Editor: pyright (Pylance) · CI: `mypy src/` (fail build on errors).
- Adopt gradually: loose → `disallow_untyped_defs` → strict.
